(p-350) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Tafsir (explanation) of Surah al-Mulk

It is Meccan by consensus. "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to recite it every night before lying down to sleep," narrated by a group [of narrators] traced back (marfu') to Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, may Allah be pleased with him. It is also related from him that he said: "Indeed, it shall save [its reciter] from the punishment of the grave, and it shall plead on behalf of its reciter until he is not punished." It is also reported that in the Torah there is a Surah al-Mulk; whoever recites it in a night has done well and good. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I wish that the surah of ﴿Blessed is He in whose hand is dominion﴾ were in the heart of every believer."

The words of the Mighty and Majestic:

﴿Blessed is He in whose hand is dominion, and He is over all things competent.﴾ ﴿He who created death and life that He may test you [as to] which of you is best in deed; and He is the Exalted in Might, the Forgiving.﴾ ﴿He who created seven heavens in layers. You do not see in the creation of the Most Merciful any inconsistency. So return your vision; do you see any flaw?﴾ ﴿Then return your vision twice; your vision will return to you humbled while it is fatigued.﴾

"Tabaraka" is a reflexive form (tafa'ala), from al-barakah, which is the increase in goodness. "Yatabarak" and "mutabarik" are not used. (p-351) His saying, the Exalted: "in His hand is the dominion" is an expression for the affirmation of sovereignty, because the hand, in the usage of human beings, is the instrument of possession, so it is used metaphorically for that. "Al-mulk" in absolute terms is that which does not perish and from which nothing becomes defective, and that is the dominion of Allah, the Exalted. The intended meaning in this verse is "King of kings," and it is like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Say: O Allah, Owner of sovereignty﴾ [Aal 'Imran: 26]. Al-Tha'labi mentioned it from Ibn 'Abbas. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿over all things competent﴾ [al-Tahrim: 8] is general, and "shay'" (thing) in linguistic usage means "that which exists."

"Death and life" are two meanings that alternate upon the body of a living being; one of them is removed by the arrival of the other. As for what has come in the hadith of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Death will be brought on the Day of Resurrection in the form of a white-speckled ram, and it will be slaughtered upon the Bridge," the people of knowledge said: that is a representation of a ram, upon which Allah, the Exalted, places necessary knowledge for the people of both abodes that it is the death which they feared in the world. That representation carries death in the sense that death is placed within it, so its life departs from it. Then Allah, the Exalted, couples the slaughter of that representation with the annihilation of death. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He created death and life that He may test you﴾ means: that He may examine you during life and recompense you after death. Abu Qatadah—and similar is related from Ibn 'Umar—said: "I said, O Messenger of Allah, what is the meaning of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿that He may test you [as to] which of you is best in deed﴾?" He said: "He, the Exalted, says: which of you is best in intellect, most fearful of Allah, the Exalted, and best in regard to His command and prohibition in consideration, even if they are least in voluntary acts." Ibn 'Abbas, Sufyan al-Thawri, and al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: "Which of you is best in deed": most ascetic of you in the world. His saying, the Exalted: "liyabluwakum" (that He may test you) indicates an action whose implied meaning is: "then He sees or knows which of you." A group of the interpreters said: "death and life" are an expression for this world and the Hereafter. He called this "death" from the perspective that death is in it, and He called that "life" from the perspective that (p-352) there is no death in it. So He described them with the two verbal nouns, with the omission of a modifier understood, as in "adl (justice) and zur (falsehood)." He placed death first in the wording because it is prior in the soul, in awe and severity.

"Tibaqan" (in layers): al-Zajjaj said: it is a verbal noun. It was also said: it is the plural of tabaqah or the plural of tabaq, like rahbah and rihab, or jabal and jibal. The meaning: some of them above others. Aban ibn Taghlib said: "I heard a Bedouin disparaging a man, and he said: his evil is layered, and his good is not lasting." As for what some commentators mentioned about the heavens, that some of them are of gold, silver, ruby, and the like, all of this is weak, and no hadith has been established concerning it. No human being knows the reality of this.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿You do not see in the creation of the Most Merciful any inconsistency﴾ means: [no] lack of proportion, and [no] departure from agreement. The inconsistent matter is that which exceeds its limits, whether by excess or deficiency. The majority of reciters read "min tafawut," while Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Ibn Mas'ud, 'Alqamah, al-Aswad, Ibn Jubayr, Talhah, and al-A'mash read "min tafawwut," and both have one meaning. Some scholars said: "fi khalq al-Rahman" refers only to the heavens, which are what the wording includes, and it is these that He intended by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Do you see any flaw?﴾, and by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿your vision will return to you﴾ and so on. They said: otherwise there are flaws in the earth. Others said: "fi khalq al-Rahman" refers to all that Allah, the Exalted, has created of things, for there is no inconsistency or flaw in them, as they proceed in perfect order; and whenever there are flaws that do not corrupt the created thing as the thing it is, but rather are a perfection within it, then those are not the ones intended in the verse. Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: Allah, the Exalted, commanded looking at the sky and its creation, then He commanded repeating the looking; likewise, all created things: whenever an observer looks at them in order to see in them a defect or deficiency, his vision will return humbled and fatigued. "Al-Hasir" is the one who is weary and exhausted; from it is the poet's saying:

﴾ Their hooves, if they were a help in the parting, and there is still a limping and weary one among them. ﴿

From this is the Arabs' saying: "So-and-so is sālim al-ghayb," meaning he is not harmed. So the meaning is: they act in accordance with fear in their prayers, their acts of worship, and when alone. The first possibility is praise for sincerity and faith; the second is praise for righteous deeds in private, and that is more fitting for them to perform openly.

The Exalted's words: ﴿And conceal your speech or disclose it﴾ address all of creation. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) said: the occasion of its revelation was that some polytheists said to others: "Conceal your speech, lest Muhammad hear you." So the meaning is that the matter is the same before Allah the Exalted, for He knows what passes through the heart without its being uttered, so how much more so when it is spoken secretly or openly. "Dhāt al-ṣudūr" means what is within them. This is like the saying: "The wolf is envied for the one in its belly," and its explanation has been given more than once before.

The Exalted's words: ﴿Should He not know, He who created?﴾ People differed over the grammatical case of "man" (who). Some grammarians said its case is nominative, as if the Exalted said: "Does the Creator not know His creation?" On this view the object is omitted. Others said its case is accusative, as if He said: "Does Allah not know whom He created?" Makki said: People of deviation have clung to this interpretation, because it implies that those whom Allah the Exalted created are the servants, since He said "man," and thus actions would be excluded from that, for the Mu'tazilah say that servants create their own actions. Their clinging to this interpretation is weak, and the dispute with the Mu'tazilah over the question of the creation of actions has a different basis, because this verse is evidence for them and against them.

"Dhalūl" is fa'ūl in the sense of maf'ūl, meaning madhlūlah (made tractable), so it is like rakūb and ḥalūb. It is said: dhalūl (with a kasra on the dhāl) means clearly tractable, and dhalīl (with a ḍammah on the dhāl) means clearly humbled.

The exegetes differed over the meaning of "al-manākib." Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) said: its manākib are its extremities, which are the mountains. Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: its sides, which are its regions. Mujahid said: they are its tracts and wide passages. This last view accords with the language, because they incline to the right and left, and the one walking in them walks in their manākib.

This verse enumerates blessings in making the people's dealings easy and in enjoying the provision of Allah the Exalted. "Al-nushūr" is life after death.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 67, verse 16–20:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿Are you secure from He who is in the heaven that He will cause the earth to swallow you, and then it will shake?﴾ ﴿Or are you secure from He who is in the heaven that He will send against you a storm of pebbles? Then you will know how My warning was.﴾ ﴿And those before them had denied, so how was My rejection?﴾ ﴿Have they not considered the birds above them, spreading out their wings and folding them in? None holds them up except the Most Merciful. Indeed, He is Seeing of all things.﴾ ﴿Who is it that is an army for you to support you other than the Most Merciful? The disbelievers are only in delusion.﴾

ʿĀṣim, Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī and Ibn ʿĀmir read "ʾa-amintum" with two clearly articulated hamzas and no elongation. Abū ʿAmr and Nāfiʿ read "al-nushūr ʾāmintum" with one hamza and an elongation. Ibn Kathīr read "al-nushūr wa-amintum," changing the hamza into a waw because it follows a ḍammah, and with an elongation after the waw.

His saying, "Man fī al-samāʾ" (He who is in the heaven), follows the customary way in which human beings receive the commands of God Most High, and the descent of decree with its events, its blessings, its punishments and its signs from that direction. For this reason, the raising of hands and faces in supplication became directed toward that direction and that side. "Khasf al-arḍ" (the swallowing up of the earth) means that it goes down into the depths. "Tamūr" means that it sways and moves, as dust is carried away by the wind, and as blood moves and surges. From this is the saying of the Bedouin: "And she left the ground in motion (mawran)."

"Al-ḥāṣib" is hail and what is similar to it, because in the language it is the wind that hurls pebbles (ḥaṣbāʾ). From this is the saying of al-Farazdaq:

Facing the north of Syria, they are pelted by a storm like scattered cotton fluff.

Jumhūr al-sabʿah read "fa-sataʿlamūna" with a tāʾ. al-Kisāʾī alone read "fa-sayaʿlamūna" with a yāʾ. The seven and others read "nadhīr" without a yāʾ, according to their method with the verse endings (fawāṣil), which resemble rhyme (qawāfī). Nāfiʿ, in the narration of Warsh alone, read "nadhīrī" with a yāʾ, according to the original form, and likewise in "nakīrī." "Al-nakīr" is likewise. From this is the saying of Ḥassān ibn Thābit:

So he warned Quraysh with a similar sincere counsel, from the Most Merciful, if you accept my warning.

Then He referred to the lesson in the matter of the birds and the perfection of their creation, and this shows the impotence of the idols and images. "Ṣāffāt" is the plural of "ṣāffah," which is the one that spreads its wings and extends them until it seems still. "Qabḍ al-janāḥ" (folding of the wing) is drawing it to the side. From this is the saying of Abū Khirāsh:

... it moves the wing between spreading and folding.

These are two states of the bird, and it rests from one of them to the other. His saying, Exalted is He, "wa-yaqbiḍna" is the coordination of the imperfect verb with the active participle, as a poet coordinated the active participle with the imperfect verb in his saying:

He spent the night covering them with a cutting, sharp sword, aiming at their path and their deviation.

(p-360) Ṭalḥah ibn Muṣarrif read "amana" with a lightened mīm in this one, and read the one after it with a heavy mīm like the community. "Al-jund" are a man's helpers in his undertakings. His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He, "in al-kāfirūna illā fī ghurūr" is an address to Muḥammad (ﷺ) after an affirmation: Say to them, O Muhammad: "Who is this..."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 67, verses 21–25:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿Or who is this that could provide for you if He withheld His provision? Nay, but they persist in insolence and aversion.﴾ ﴿Is one who walks prone on his face better guided, or one who walks upright on a straight path?﴾ ﴿Say: "It is He who brought you into being and made for you hearing, sight and hearts; little thanks do you give.﴾ ﴿Say: "It is He who multiplied you upon the earth, and to Him you will be gathered."﴾ ﴿And they say: "When is this promise, if you are truthful?"﴾

This too is a challenge concerning a matter in which the idols have no part. By "provision" is meant rain, because it is the greatest of provisions. Then God, exalted is He, informed about them that they persisted and continued in refusing to obey God, the Exalted; this is "ʿutuw" (insolence). "Nufur" (aversion) is distancing oneself from the truth swiftly and hastily. It is said: nafara ʿan al-amr nufūran, and nafara ilā al-amr nafīran, and the animal bolted (nafarat al-dābba nifāran).

The exegetes (ahl al-ta'wil) differed concerning the occasion of revelation of His saying: ﴿Is one who walks prone﴾, the verse. A group of narrators of occasions of revelation (ruwat al-asbab) said: it was revealed as a parable for Hamza ibn ʿAbd al-Muttalib, may Allah be pleased with him, and for Abu Jahl ibn Hisham. Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn al-Kalbi and others said: it was revealed as a parable for Muhammad (ﷺ) and Abu Jahl ibn Hisham. Ibn ʿAbbas also said, along with Mujahid and al-Dahhak: it was revealed concerning the believers and the disbelievers in general. Qatada said: it was revealed informing about the states of the Resurrection, and that the disbelievers will walk on their faces therein, while the believers walk upright. "It was said to the Prophet (ﷺ): How does the disbeliever walk on his face? He said: 'The One who made him walk on his two feet in this world is able to make him walk on his face in the Hereafter.'"

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

So the disbelievers stood between the two states at that time. In the first three opinions, walking is figurative, imagined; in the fourth opinion it is literal, occurring on the Day of Resurrection.

It is said: "akabba al-rajul" when he turned his face toward the ground, and "kabbahu" means "ghabbarahu" (made him dust-covered). He, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Do people get thrown into the Fire on their faces (ʿala mikhārihim) except as the harvest of their tongues?" This verb is an exception to the pattern: aknaba (af'ala) is intransitive, while kabba (fa'ala) is transitive; its parallel is "qashaʿat al-rīḥu al-saḥāba fa-inqashaʿa" (the wind scattered the clouds and they dispersed). And "ahdā" in this verse is an "af'al" form from "al-hudā" (guidance).

Talha read: "Amman yamshī" with the mim lightened. God used the singular for hearing (al-sam') because it is a collective noun which applies to few and many. "Qalīlan" is put in the accusative by a hidden verb, and "mā" is a verbal-noun particle (maṣdariyya), in a place of nominative case. His saying: ﴿little thanks do you give﴾ — its apparent meaning requires that they give a little thanks. This may mean either that whatever thanks a disbeliever may have is little and ineffective, or that he intends to negate thanks from them entirely, expressing it by the cause, as the Arabs say: "This is a land that rarely produces such-and-such," while it does not produce it at all. And among the thanks of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) for this blessing was that he used to say in his prostration: "My face prostrates to the One who created it, shaped it, and split its hearing and sight."

"Dhara'akum" means: He scattered you. The "gathering" referred to is the resurrection of the Last Day, and to it He pointed with His saying: ﴿this promise﴾. So God informed that they were hastening the matter of the Resurrection and demanding certainty about the truth of that report.
